text: Ivan the Fourth became ruler of Moscow when he was three years old.
When he was seven, his mother died suddenly. Many believed she was poisoned.
For years, rival noble families, the boyars, fought over the boy and the palace. Ivan later wrote that they ignored him, stole from the treasury, and sometimes didn't even feed him.
[grim] This is not going to end well.
In fifteen forty-seven, at sixteen, Ivan did something new. He had himself crowned Tsar. From the Roman word Caesar.
And at first, he was... actually good. New laws, a standing army, and big wins: he conquered the Tatar cities of Kazan and Astrakhan, opening the whole Volga to Moscow.
To celebrate Kazan, he built the famous colourful cathedral on Red Square: Saint Basil's.
[pointing at the domes] That one. The one that looks like a bowl of ice cream.
Then, in fifteen sixty, his beloved wife Anastasia died. Ivan was sure she had been poisoned. And something in him broke.
He created the Oprichnina: a private police force dressed in black, riding with a dog's head and a broom on their saddles.
[whispering] The dog's head meant "we sniff out traitors". The broom meant "we sweep them away".
They terrorised the country. In fifteen seventy, Ivan's men massacred thousands in the city of Novgorod, on suspicion of treason.
Then came the worst moment of all. In fifteen eighty-one, during a furious argument, Ivan struck his own son and heir with his iron-tipped staff.
The young man died days later. Ivan never recovered from it.
[timid] Your Majesty... the ambassador from England is here.
[growling] Is he loyal?
He's... English, sire.
[squinting] Suspicious.
When Ivan died in fifteen eighty-four, Russia was bigger than ever. Even Siberia had begun to open, thanks to a Cossack adventurer called Yermak.
But the country was exhausted, terrified, and broke. And the next tsar, Ivan's son Feodor, was gentle, pious... and had no children.
[checking his watch] Total control went too far. You know what comes next.
Feodor died in fifteen ninety-eight. And with him, the family of Rurik, after more than seven hundred years, was gone.
Russians literally named the next fifteen years the Time of Troubles.
First, a powerful noble called Boris Godunov grabbed the throne. Then the weather turned against him.
Around sixteen hundred and one, frosts and rain wrecked the harvest three years in a row. A terrible famine killed a huge part of the population.
And then a young man appeared in Poland with an incredible claim.
[grandly] I am Dmitry, the lost son of Ivan the Terrible!
[doubtful] Didn't Dmitry die as a child?
[confidently] I got better.
[shrugging] Good enough. Here's an army.
The real Dmitry had died in fifteen ninety-one. But the False Dmitry marched on Moscow with Polish support, and when Boris suddenly died, Moscow let him in. He was crowned tsar.
Within a year, angry boyars killed him. The story goes that his body was burned, and his ashes were fired from a cannon back towards Poland.
[covering his eyes] That's one way to return to sender.
Then came another tsar. Then a second False Dmitry. Then the Swedes invaded. Then, in sixteen ten, the Polish army marched into Moscow and took the Kremlin itself.
Russia had no tsar, no government, and a foreign army in its heart.
And then, something unusual happened. Ordinary people fixed it.
In the city of Nizhny Novgorod, a meat trader named Kuzma Minin started collecting money for a people's army, and asked a wounded prince, Dmitry Pozharsky, to lead it.
In sixteen twelve, they drove the Poles out of Moscow. Russia still celebrates that day as a national holiday.
[impressed] A butcher saving the country. Respect.
In sixteen thirteen, an assembly chose a new tsar: a shy sixteen-year-old named Michael Romanov.
His family would rule Russia for the next three hundred and four years.
Chaos, again, had produced order. The loop was complete. Time for the next one.
